A car was pushed off a bridge and into the St. Francois River at State Highway U and County Road 31. Water was covering the bridge at the time.
Heavy rain caused water to run over Route CC near Highway 21 and Route E east of Potosi.
MO-14 was closed due to flash flooding.

Route AB at Wolf Creek was closed due to flooding. Additional county property damages were reported throughout the entire county, primarily to dirt roads and bridges. Damage cost estimates are a reflection of the county as a whole.
High water covered Highway 165 and Crawford Loop just south of Pollock.
High water covered Highway 167 and Thigpen Road near the Bentley community.
The intersection of Highway 122 and 123 was flooded in Dry Prong.
Delayed Report: Video via broadcast media showing a retention pond overflowing across a roadway near Coursey Blvd and a nearby retail store caused by heavy rainfall.
Street flooding up to the upper part of the tires on a truck in the Belle Savanne subdivision in Geismar.
Southwest of Cisco, CR 145 and CR 187 were closed due to flooding.
A home was reported as flooded near the Jack/Wise County line off of US Hwy 380.
Water was reported over the road at 1st Ave and 3rd Street.
Water was reported over the roadway at Airport Road and Dillon Road.
Dawson Creek rose out of its banks and caused flooding along Williams Creek Road in Norton Branch.
An amateur radio operator relayed a report that water was flowing over KY-1064 by Sargent's Pay Lake. Fire Department was on scene and the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet had been notified.

Heavy rain resulted in releases from Watauga Dam that began to flash flood garages and yards of riverside homes along Watauga Drive in Elizabethton around 10:30 am EST. Flash flooding flowing down the Doe River from the Roan Mountain vicinity began to flood homes and roads in the Valley Forge area around 11:25 am EST. Flooding of areas near the Doe River in Elizabethton began around 11:45 am EST when the stage exceeded 9.5 feet. Much of Elizabethton along either side of North Main and South Main Streets flooded as the Doe exceeded 10 feet. Billy Bob Garrison Field had as much as two feet of water. Homes and businesses flooded on North East Street (adjacent to North Main), where vehicles were moved and flipped by flood waters. At 1:50 pm EST, Sycamore Shoals Hospital on the west side of Elizabethton was evacuated. The Doe River and its flash flooding impacts peaked at 1:30 pm EST with a crest of 10.78 feet, and fell below 9.5 feet at 4 pm EST. The Watauga River crested at 13.57 feet at 2:15 pm EST, and flooding continued into the next day.
Horse Creek Park Road near TN 107 had six inches of water across it. Small streams in the area were over their banks.
Flooding observed in several locations in and around Jonesborough.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding. There was a high water rescue of a vehicle stranded on Blanco Rd. at Meusebach Creek near Camp Bullis.
Thunderstorms produced an estimated two to five inches of rain in three hours. This rain caused flash flooding closing Little Blanco Rd. near Twin Sisters.
Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding closing roads in northwestern San Antonio.

Flash flooding resulted in cropland, yard, basement, and road flooding around Jefferson County. Water flooded residences in a mobile home park in High Ridge, with several homes and mobile homes being evacuated. Multiple water rescues were also reported in House Springs.

Highway Y at Cowskin Creek was closed due to flooding. Additional county property damages were reported throughout the entire county, primarily to dirt roads and bridges. Damage cost estimates are a reflection of the county as a whole.
Hooper Road near Gone Wild Safari near the Grant/Rapides Parish line was flooded.
Hughart Road near Highway 8 near the Pollock community was flooded.
Mayo Road south of Highway 8 west of Jena was covered in high water.
Photo via broadcast media of high water over Cypress Swamp Drive in the Moss Pointe area of Dutchtown.

Numerous streets and highways were flooded across Alexandria, Pineville, Ball, Union Hill, and Deville with some impassable. Some vehicles stalled in the floodwaters. Multiple structures had water approach, but no homes took in water. Rainfall totals exceeded 8 inches.
Black Creek at Highway 326 reached minor flood stage. This produced minor flooding of several roadways near Black Creek.
A home was reported as flooded in the 2000 block of Dark Corner Road. This location is south of US Hwy 380, about half way between Bryson and Jacksboro.
The Sunset VFD reported flooding on State Hwy 101 near the Big Sandy Creek Bridge.
Nocona Hills VFD conducted a high water rescue on Rivercrest Drive near Lake Nocona.
A few mPING reports of street flooding and road closures were reported in Temple.
Public reported on social media that there were flooded roads near Fannin Elementary.
Public reported on social media that there was flash flooding on Main Street in San Angelo.
Public reported that there was water over Irving Street in downtown San Angelo and measured 3 feet of water at a staff gage at the intersection of Avenue Q and Chadbourne.
Water was reported over the roadway at Highway 319N and Sanford Road.
Water was over the roadway on Highway 107.

Multiple flooded roadways were observed across the county. This included along Poplar Street in Flatwoods, where high water flooded the porch of a home and came close to entering the house. Another home observed water entering their home along Amanda Furnace Drive in Bellefonte. High water was also observed at the intersection of Argillite Road and Turley Avenue in Flatwoods.
Flooding of Maples Branch Road as well as Red Bank Road.
Flooding of the parking lot of Bethel Baptist Church. Water touched the back corner of the brick wall of the education building.
McCollough Cemetery Road and Bulls Gap St. Clair Road were closed due to flooding in Bulls Gap.

Heavy rain caused numerous road closures with vehicles stranded in St. Louis County. Multiple water rescues were reported from cars driving through flooded roadways. At Bayless and I-55, flash flooding from heavy rain and overflow from Gravois Creek resulted in two fatalities.

Trained spotters reported the intersection of Washington Avenue and Broadway Street in West Plains was impassable due to flash flooding. Additional county property damages were reported throughout the entire county, primarily to dirt roads and bridges. Damage cost estimates are a reflection of the county as a whole.
Emergency Manager reported that a water rescue was performed off of County Road 9100 near Spring Creek.
The Avoyelles Parish EM reported Highway 114 and 115 was flooded around Hessmer and Marksville. Roads from Marksville to Deville were also flooded.
Social media report that the Aiken Department of Public Safety closed Whiskey Road between Knox Ave. and Grace Ave. due to flooding.
Social media report that the Aiken Department of Public Safety closed the intersection of University Parkway and Vaucluse Rd. due to flooding.
Portions of Florida Blvd in Mandeville flooded with a few stalled vehicles.
Several roads were flooded in the Tifton area.
A structure on Pate Street had a couple of inches of water in it due to flash flooding.
Significant amounts of high water were observed along Route 7 and throughout the town of South Shores.
Deep water ponding on Dyke Street in Andover.
Water was flowing across Trapping Brook Road.

As the north and northeastern eyewall stretched into an east-west oriented band of heavy rainfall, training storms resulted in widespread rainfall totals of 5-7 inches across the northern half of the parish. Radar estimates indicate locally higher totals of up to 10 inches may have fallen in some areas. Much of the rain fell within a short span of only a couple hours, resulting in widespread flash flooding throughout areas such as Thibodaux, Chackbay and Kraemer. Numerous roads became impassable, 30 homes flooded, and 26 residents were rescued from their flooded homes.

Heavy rain of 5-7��� also fell across the parish with locally higher amounts. Much of this rain fell over the course of just a few hours, resulting in significant flash flooding, especially from Covington through Slidell. Numerous roads became impassable and several homes were flooded. In total, approximately 20 homes were flooded either from the heavy rain or storm surge.

Flooding along portions of Hwy 19 was reported at 8:00 am EST. Reports from spotters, social media, broadcast media, and county officials increased through the day, including flooded roadways at 8:51 am EST. Flooding of the Nolichucky River at the Jackson Love Hwy bridge area was noted at 9:32 am EST. Flooding of the grounds around Unicoi Hospital was happening around 10:00 am EST, when a berm was overtopped or breached. The hospital structure was taking water by 11:00 am EST, and evacuation by ground had become unsafe. Occupants were taken to the roof, but winds prevented air rescue while rapidly rising and turbulent river flooding prevented water rescue. The hospital was surrounded and inundated by waters at least 7 feet deep by 12:45 pm EST. Flood waters inundated numerous nearby properties and structures including a church, wrecked nearby portions of I-26, and caused significant damage to factories along the river downstream. Hospital occupants were at last rescued by helicopter in the afternoon. Nine known fatalities found in the county; the final three in the list were North Carolina residents, and it is unknown if they were in Unicoi county when they perished or if they were swept in from North Carolina. Most of the deaths were workers swept from a factory parking lot. Flooding impacts continued across the county through the night.
Bulloch County dispatch reported flood waters entering two homes just west of Statesboro. One home was on Hodges Circle and the other was on W Jones Avenue.
Heavy rain caused water over major roadways such as I-44 at Nebraska Ave and I-70 at Carrie Avenue. On Skinker Blvd, vehicles were stranded due to flash flooding.
Emergency Management reported that a water rescue was performed on County Road 1280 due to a flooded out car.
The Fire Department conducted a water rescue on Highway 17 between Roby and Success. The road was under construction, and developed large pot holes due to the flood waters washing away the roadway.
The bridge at Dogs Bluff Access on Highway 17 was reported flooded. The fire department said water has never overtopped this bridge before.
A social media image shows significant roadway flooding near the intersection of Southwest 51st Street and Douglas Avenue. Event time is approximate.
Reports from the public of several streets with several inches of water on the roadways and a few streets with minor flooding.
Public reports water inside Northshore High School, roughly 1-3 inches inside the halls of the building.
Flooding across Soult St near the corner of Labarre St and Soult St.
Flooding at the entrance to the Woodlands along Soult St.
Ephesus Church Road was flooded with water over the roadway.
Shingler Road was flooded north of Ephesus Church Road.
Portion of Traux Road washed out, Funland Skate Center inundated with waters, flooding on Trapping Brook Road and North Broad Street in Wellsville.

There were several reports of flash flooding in the city of Brownsville, mainly bracketed by Price Road and Expressway IH-69E on the west, Price Road and State Highway 48 on the east, extending to the Southmost neighborhood on the south side of the city. Reports included: Multiple intersections along Boca Chica Blvd impassable due to flooded roadways between McDavitt Blvd and Kings Hwy and Boca Chica was nearly impassable, as well as the intersection known as Four Corners at State Highway 4; flooding extending along State Highway 4 to Southmost Blvd., and flooding along and near the frontage road at Price Road and IH-69E, extending to Barnard Road, and to nearby apartment complexes and shopping centers in this area.||While all locations inside the ascribed polygon may not have reached flash flood levels - 3 feet or higher of ponded water - the reports of impassible roads and photographic evidence suggesting pockets of this level of water depth made the case for a flash flood event in these areas.||Damage to any property was unknown as of this writing.

Large event that began with roads blocked by flooding. Water quickly began encroaching into low-lying structures and residences especially in and near Damascus during late morning, especially along Laurel Creek, which runs through town. Evacuations and water rescues were underway before noon EDT (11 am EST). Laurel Creek rose five feet in an hour, from near 9.75 feet to near 14.75 feet from 10:30 am to 11:30 am EDT (9:30 to 10:30 am EST). Gage was destroyed when its bridge collapsed, but probably after measuring near 17 feet at 12:15 pm EDT (11:15 am EST). The river continued to rise probably another foot or two. Residents continued calling 911 due to flooding of homes and roads through midafternoon, with some of the structures being destroyed. Water rescues continued. There is conjecture that the bridge with the stream gage, located upstream from town, was partially dammed by debris, and when the bridge collapsed, it contributed to a secondary rapid rise in Damascus. A mudslide occurred behind a residence during the early evening. Damaged estimates include $15 million in agriculture, $4 million on destroyed dwellings, $1 million on various expenses, and $100 million to repair the famed Creeper Trail.

The greater impact was from Francine���s flooding rain, though. As the north and northeastern eyewall stretched into an east-west oriented band of heavy rainfall, training storms resulted in widespread rainfall totals of 7-9��� across the parish with locally higher amounts, much of which fell over the course of just a couple hours. The heavy rain resulted in significant flash flooding across the parish, with numerous areas becoming inaccessible, and approximately over 350 homes and businesses being flooded throughout the parish, with the worst flooding reported in Norco.
The storm produced widespread rainfall totals of 3-4 inches across the parish, with higher totals of 5-7��� in the far southern portion of the parish.

Flash flooding on the Nolichucky River flowed downstream from Unicoi County. This stretch of the river is a gorge that opens into the flood plain of the Bumpus Cove Road section of the town of Embreeville. Water rescue operations had begun by 9:00 am EST in Embreeville. The stream gauge in Embreeville crossed the 16 foot moderate flood stage around 9:07 am EST. Flooding of low spots along TN 107 between Embreeville and Erwin began around 9:30 am EST. By 10:00 am EST water was beginning to threaten Embreeville homes along the river on Bumpus Cove Road as the river reached 18 feet. The river reached the 20 foot major flood stage shortly after 10:30 am EST, and water was entering some of those Bumpus Cove Road homes. The river gauge at this time was destroyed. The river crested at 33.88 feet during the afternoon (as determined later by high water marks), nearly 10 feet above the previous all-time record crest. Practically every home on Bumpus Cove Road in Embreeville was destroyed. The KOA Campground was destroyed, and even its main building at the highest point in the campground near the highway was substantially damaged. The flood waters progressed downstream all day through Washington County, wiping out homes and structures and bridges and roadways and agricultural land along its path. The threats and impacts of the flood continued through the night.

Heavy rainfall resulted in flooding across north-central portions of Kay County. This included significant roadway flooding along portions of Oklahoma State Highway 11 and U.S. Highway 77 near the communities of Blackwell and Newkirk. Event time is approximate.
Roadway flooding across a portion of U.S. Highway 377 north of the community of Fittstown. At least one vehicle stranded. Event time is approximate.
Pictures on social media showed several inches of water flowing over Blanton Branch Road near the communities of Kettle Island and Jenson.
Pictures on social media showed several inches of water flowing down Kettle Island Branch Road, a few hundred feet downstream from Newton Branch Road, near the community of Kettle Island.
Pictures on social media showed flooding along KY-987, a half mile from the US-119/KY-987 intersection, just east of the Calvin community.
Multiple law enforcement and emergency management confirmations of roadway flooding in and around the community of Cache. Event time is approximate.
The river gauge at Oberlin indicated the Calcasieu briefly exceeded bank full and flooded nearby fields and roads.
Water approached some homes in the Sulphur area with numerous streets flooded in Sulphur, Moss Bluff, and Lake Charles during the storm. Some road ways were closed as water became too deep.
A vehicle had to be rescued along Raider Hollow Road. The vehicle was not on the road at the time of the rescue, but had fallen into a water-filled ditch along the side of the road.
Portions of U.S. Highway 177 flooded, from the U.S. Highway 60 intersection to the community of Blackwell. Portions of the roadway may have been washed out as well. Event time is approximate.
The bridge over Sulphur Creek along Purdy Sano Road was destroyed by flood waters.
Flash flooding occurred in multiple locations along Sulphur Creek, causing several roads which cross the creek to become impassable. Some roads which cross the creek were damaged by flood waters.
Flooding across all lanes of Interstate 35 near mile marker 217. Event time is approximate.
Liberty Road was impassable due to flood waters from Sulphur Creek.
Roadway flooding along Oklahoma State Highway 5, near the Tillman and Cotton County line. Relayed by emergency management. Event time is approximate.

Thunderstorms with heavy rainfall went through the Tucson Metro on August 8th resulting in 0.5 to 1.0 inches of rain leading to flash flooding and running washes. In addition, the Pima County Medical Examiner found that drowning was the primary factor in the death of one individual. The individual was found in Aviation Wash on August 9th with debris and running water.

Spotter reported street flooding and basements being flooded in Yuma. Pictures from other sources show hail accumulating to around a foot deep. The combined affects of deep hail and heavy rainfall likely overwhelmed the storm drains, preventing the heavy rainfall from draining away. Unclear how many basements were flooded, or how much damage was caused by the flooding.

A stream gauge on the Cullasaja River in the Gneiss community indicated flash flooding developed along the lower portion of the river after 10-15 inches of rain fell across the headwaters over three days. 1.5 to 3.5 inches of that fell in less than six hours during the early morning of the 27th. Portions of River Rd and Fulton Rd were inundated, with water entering several homes along River Rd near Peaceful Cove Rd. A couple of campgrounds and RV parks were also inundated. A 75-year-old man was killed when he drove his vehicle into floodwater on Fulton Rd.

A stream gauge on the Catawba River at Lookout Shoals Dam indicated flash flooding developed in the vicinity of the damn after widespread extremely heavy rainfall occurred in the upper part of the basin across the mountains and foothills over three days, with 6-9 inches falling across Catawba County. More than 100 structures were damaged on the Catawba County side of the river, especially in the Carpenters Cover community. Numerous roads were inundated and damaged as well. The gauge at Lookout Shoals reached its highest level since August 1940.

A stream gauge on the Tuckasegee River in Bryson City indicated flash flooding developed along the stream after 4 to 8 inches of rain, with locally higher amounts fell across the county in around two days. Through mid-morning, impacts were limited to inundation of a couple of campgrounds and other low-lying spots. Several people has to be rescued from one of these campgrounds as the water rose too quickly for them to evacuate.

A stream gauge on Lyle Creek in the Conover area indicated flash flooding developed along the stream after 6 to 10 inches of rain fell across the area in around three days, with 1 to 2 inches of that falling in less than six hours during the morning of the 27th. Water entered around a half dozen homes while inundating several streets between Section House Rd and County Home Rd.

An short-duration but high-intensity thunderstorm passed across the City of Martinsville, bringing 2 to 2.5 inches of rain in less than an hour. The intensity of rainfall overwhelmed storm drains, causing water to back up onto several city streets. Multiple roads became flooded and impassible by several inches of flowing water, and remained closed until the water drained away, with no damage to the roadways reported. About 6 inches of water was observed flowing across the intersection of Memorial Boulevard and Bridge Street. At least one road was flooded near Southside Park, with multiple vehicles becoming stranded in the floodwaters while attempting to drive through it. The damage estimate is the damage caused to vehicles becoming stranded in the flood waters.

A stream gauge on the Saluda River in west Greenville indicated flash flooding developed along the river after 8-15 inches of rain fell across the foothills in three days, with 1.5 to 2.5 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. Multiple homes and structures were inundated and damaged on the Pickens County side of the river in east Easley, including on Shop Ct, Shady Acres Circle, Covenant Dr, and Easley Bridge Rd.

A slow moving thunderstorm produced about four inches of rain within a 75-minute period, with rates approaching five inches per hour. At 7 pm EDT, CREST Unit Flow peaked at an exceptional 2,612 cfs/mi^2, while rainfall amounts rose to 220 percent of Flash Flood Guidance. Runoff from this rainfall caused several roads in the Ajax area through Gretna area of Pittsylvania County to become flooded and impassible until the water receded, including Jasmine Road (Highway 778), Sandy Road, Grassland Drive and West Gretna Road. Millstream Drive was reported washed out by Georges Creek, making the road impassible until repairs can be completed. Whitehorn Creek reportedly overflowed its bank across Chalk Level Road, making the road impassible until the flooding receded. At least four other roads, names unknown, were flooded and impassible along the western and northwestern sides of Gretna.

Slow moving thunderstorms produced between 2 and 2.5 inches of rainfall across central Campbell County during the evening of September 30th, with rain at times falling at a rate of four inches per hour. The CREST Unit Flow peaked at 270 cfs/mi^2, while rainfall estimates were 70 to 80 percent of Flash Flood Guidance. Regardless, the short but intense rainfall was enough to produce runoff that flooded multiple roads, making them impassible for short periods of time: Depot Street, Crows Road, Brookneal Highway near Gladys, and Campbell Highway in Rustburg. Flooding also occurred along Village Highway, where one vehicle was washed off the road, as well as along Rocky Road. It is uncertain if there was any damage to the vehicle. No damage to the roads were reported.
Pembrook Road was flooded and impassible as Town Creek overflowed its banks several inches deep across the road.

A stream gauge on the Broad River at Bat Cave indicated flash flooding developed, with over a one-foot rise in less than an hour, after 3 to 5 inches of rain fell across the basin in less than 6 hours. Multiple campgrounds and the crawl spaces of a few homes were inundated from Bat Cave and vicinity downstream to the Rutherford County line.

A stream gauge on Cane Creek in the Bakersville area exceeded its established flood stage after 3 to 4 inches of rain fell across the area in around three hours. Multiple roads in Bakersville and vicinity were inundated, including a portion of Highway 226.

Isolated flash flooding developed over southwest Alexander County after 8 to 12 inches of rain fell across the county over a couple of days. Ham radio operator reported water was flowing over the road near Devil Track Rd and Highway 127 due to Jumping Run leaving its banks. Fire Dept reported water from Stirewalt Creek flowing over a broad stretch of Heavenly Acres Lane.
Runoff from heavy rainfall caused Jacobs Creek to be observed flowing nearly a foot deep across Red House Road. No damage was reported to the road, and it was open to traffic after the water receded.

Stream gauges indicated flash flooding developed along Goose Creek and Bearskin Creek in Union County after 3 to 5 inches of rain fell across the northern part of the county over a couple of days, with 1 to 2 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. Stevens Mill Rd was flooded by Goose Creek. Bearskin Creek inundated Stafford St and flooded lower portions of Dickerson Park.
Numerous homes and businesses were flooded including the Thompson Hose Company firehouse.

Reports of flash flooding on roadways and stranded vehicles near Washington Ave and Golf Course Road in Douglas. There was also a car stuck in flooded roadway at Primrose St and Washington Ave in Douglas.
Officials reported at least two residences were flooded on the first floor with several people trapped in the homes.

Widespread and massive flash flooding of Tuscarora Creek and surrounding tributaries devastated roads, homes and businesses between, and including, the villages of Woodhull and Addison. Homes were pushed off foundations and were seen floating downstream smashing into area bridges. Dozens of people were rescued from flooded homes and vehicles and displaced in temporary shelters for weeks.

Stream gauges indicated flash flooding developed along the South Fork Catawba River and at least one tributary (Catawba Creek in Gastonia) after 5 to 9 inches fell across the western Piedmont over three days. The South Fork Catawba inundated greenways and parks along the river, as well as parking lots and several roads, including Riverside Dr. Backwater effects resulted in Hoyle Creek inundating Old Willis Rd in the Dallas area. In addition, New Hope Road at Robinwood Rd in Gastonia was flooded and impassable due to poor drainage. While heavy rain and flash flooding ended across the area by early afternoon, moderate river flooding persisted until the afternoon of the 29th and the South Fork didn't fall below flood stage until the early morning of the 30th.

Runoff from continued heavy rain resulted in numerous roads becoming flooded and impassible across Alleghany County per reports from the public and from the Alleghany County 911 Dispatch Center. Rainfall totals ranging from seven to locally ten inches were observed across much of the county on the 26th, resulting in numerous flooded creeks and roads that were covered by several inches of flowing water. After a brief lull in rainfall as the Predecessor Rainfall Event concluded, allowing flooding to subside briefly, heavy rain associated with the arrival of Tropical Storm Helene moved across the county, falling at rates of one to two inches per hour. Reports include Saddle Mountain Road being washed out and destroyed near its intersection with the Blue Ridge Parkway. Along the New River, the Farmers Fish Camp Road Bridge was completely submerged by the New River, with significant damage observed on the bridge once the flooding receded.

Runoff from heavy rainfall has resulted in flooding of several roads throughout Wythe County during the morning of the 26th. The following roads were reported flooded and impassible: Old Stage Road near Low Water Bridge, Fox Den Road, Locust Hill Road, Ramsey Mountain Road, the Millers Creek area, Ridge Avenue, Crouse Hollow Road, Saint Peters Road, and multiple roads that run along the New River.

The Smyth County 911 Center reported that Staley Creek had risen significantly out of its banks, and was flooding across surrounding roads and properties. Nearly five inches of rain had fallen during the 24 hour period ending at 12 pm EDT on the 26th, causing Staley Creek to rise to bank full conditions. Heavier rain falling during the afternoon caused the creek to rise quickly out of its banks. Some homes along the creek were reported surrounded by the flood waters. A van became stalled on Highway 16 near the community of Marion in the flood waters. A Swift Water Rescue Team assisted multiple people to safety during the incident.
One to two feet of water was reported near the intersection of Warren St. and Balcerzak Dr.
Numerous roads were flooded across the county.
There were multiple reports of flooding via the Sibley County dispatch center. Township roads and culverts were damaged.

Todd County had numerous culverts washed out. The heaviest rain fell north of Clarissa. Measured 5.62 in Clarissa, 6 to 8 public reports elsewhere. There was also damage to a few structures from the flood waters, with an estimated $400,000 in total damages.

Extensive flooding of the North Toe and Nolichucky Rivers, and their tributaries, including Cane Creek developed during the overnight and early morning hours of the 27th as rainfall rates began to intensify again during the evening of the 26th. The most intense rainfall occurred just after sunrise, as the tropical rain bands near the center of Helene swept across the area. A stream gauge on Cane Creek near Bakersville reached major flood stage of 10 feet just after sunrise before it stopped reporting. Dozens of structures were inundated and damaged throughout the county, with some homes completely swept away. Numerous bridges and roads were also damaged, especially near the Yancey County line. Three-day rainfall totals were 7-12 inches across much of the county. However, amounts of 15-20 inches were reported in the extreme southern part of the county along the McDowell County line. More than 200 landslides were reported in this part of Mitchell County, with some of those causing additional damage to structures. One 41-year-old male was killed when his home was swept away along the North Toe.

Several inches of flowing water was observed passing across intersection of Howard P. Anderson and Hodges Street. Flooding was also observed along the 1000 block of Newbill School Road, making the road impassible until the flooding receded. Runoff was from an estimated 2.5 inches of rain that fell during a 75 to 90 minute period, with rainfall rates of up to 4 inches per hour at times. No damage was reported to the roadways.

Runoff from an estimated 2.5 inches of rainfall caused the 3000 block of Mount Laurel Road to be flooded and impassible until the water receded. Rainfall rates at times as the thunderstorms passed were up to 4 inches per hour. No damage was reported to the road.

Numerous roads were flooded and impassible across Rockingham County, with several of the reports concentrated to the north and east of Reidsville. This included a report of flooding along W. Harrison Street in Reidsville, where one car stalled in the high water near the intersection of W. Harrison Street and Market Street. An underpass between E. Harrison Street and W. Harrison Street was also reported flooded and impassible until the water receded. North of Reidsville, Wolf Island Creek was observed overflowing its banks across Wolf Island Road, where two people required rescue when their vehicle was washed off the road into a corn field next to the creek. No injuries were reported. No roads were reported damaged by the flooding, which were open to traffic when the flooding receded. Damage estimates are for the vehicles.

Between 1.75 and 2.5 inches of rain fell from a thunderstorm, with rainfall rates estimated to be between 3 and 4 inches per hour. Railroad Avenue was flooded and impassible due to several inches of water flowing over the roadway. The Bedford Fire Department responded to calls for three homes and an apartment building that were partially flooded, with those residents forced to evacuate.

A stream gauge on the Soque River in Clarkesville exceeded its established flood stage after 7 to 10 inches of rain fell throughout the basin over a couple of days. Pitts Park in Clarkesville and other low spots were inundated.

Stream gauges and emergency management reported significant flash flooding developed along all major river basins in central Greenville County after 8-15 inches of rain fell across the foothills in three days, with 1.5 to 2.5 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. Flash flooding developed along the Saluda River, with the stream gauge in west Greenville reaching major flood stage, indicating multiple roads and some structures were inundated, including on Riverview Circle. Moderate flooding developed along the Reedy River through the city of Greenville, with extensive flooding of the greenway from Unity Park downstream to Cleveland Park and inundation of multiple roads, including Hudson St, which was damaged and closed for months. Brushy Creek overflowed its banks on the eastside of Greenville and inundated multiple roads, including Edwards Rd, where water entered several homes and Devenger Rd. Significant flooding developed along the Enoree River, with a gauge on the river at Pelham reaching its highest level since August 1995 (Tropical Cyclone Jerry). Inundated roads along the river included Gibbs Shoals Rd.

Runoff from continued heavy rain resulted in numerous roads becoming flooded and impassible across Watauga County per reports from the public and from the Watauga County 911 Dispatch Center. Rainfall totals ranging from seven to locally 11 inches were observed across much of the county on the 26th, resulting in numerous flooded creeks, as well as several roads that were covered by several inches to feet of flowing water. After a brief lull in rainfall as the Predecessor Rainfall Event concluded early on the morning of the 27th, allowing flooding to slow down briefly, heavy rain associated with the arrival of Tropical Storm Helene moved across the county, falling at rates of one to two inches per hour. Flash flooding occurred in downtown Boone, where water flowing down the several streets rose high enough to enter nearby businesses and homes. Several streets in the Beech Mountain area were flooded and closed, with multiple streets washed out and destroyed. Multiple vehicles became stranded in the flooded roads, with some of the occupants requiring rescue by a swift water team. A total of 1,135 buildings were impacted by flooding and/or winds. Of those, 118 were completely destroyed, 479 had major damage and 538 had minor damages. Several of the destroyed homes were in the Meat Camp community. Also significantly damaged were several buildings on the Appalachian State University campus as Boone Creek, which runs through the campus, rose out of its banks and inundated mainly the classroom buildings, forcing the cancellation of classes through October 16th. It was also noted that a large sink hole formed near the Legends Building in downtown Boone. There were 220 water rescues conducted across the county, most coming from stranded automobiles, though sixpeople were rescued from building collapses. There were two known fatalities in Watauga County related flooding from Helene. One female died when a landslide washed away her home, and a second female drowned.

Runoff from between 1.5 and 2 inches of rain falling over moist soil caused the intersection of North James Madison Highway and Thomas Road to be flooded and impassible for a brief period of time. Further north, Randolph Creek Road was reported covered with flowing water, with one car trapped in the flood waters. The occupant was able to escape the vehicle on their own. Another vehicle became trapped in floodwaters along Clay Bank Road, with the occupant needing to be rescued by boat. The intersection of Ridge Road and Penlan Road was observed flooded. Near the community of Dillwyn, several inches of water was observed flowing across Rosney Road, as well as High Rocks Road where rainfall rates of up to four inches per hour were observed. Cattail Creek rose out of its banks, and was observed flowing across Plank Road near the intersection with Back Mountain Road. Allens Lake Road was washed out and destroyed when a tributary of Tower Branch overflowed its banks across the roadway. A swift water rescue was required for a vehicle that became stranded where Hunts Creek flooded across Slate Hill Road.
Several roads were flooded in Springfield, including the 1600 block of Sangamon Avenue and parts of Clock Tower Drive and Durkin Drive.

A stream gauge on the Broad River at Bat Cave indicated flash flooding developed, with over a one-foot rise in less than an hour, after 3 to 5 inches of rain fell across the basin in less than 6 hours. Multiple campgrounds and the crawl spaces of a few structures were inundated from the Henderson County line down to Lake Lure.

A stream gauge on the North Toe River at Newland exceeded its established flood stage after 1.5 to 3 inches of rain fell across the area in less than 6 hours. A portion of River St was inundated as were greenways along the river in Newland and vicinity.

Stream gauges along the Catawba River indicated flash flooding developed along the portion of the Catawba River in northeast Burke County (Rhodiss Dam and vicinity) after 7 to 13 inches of rain fell across upper much of Burke County over a three-day period. Multiple homes and some structures were inundated due to the river itself, and due to backwater effects into tributaries, including Silver Creek and Lower Creek.

Emergency management reported flash flooding developed along tributaries of the Tallulah River in south central Rabun County after 8 to 12 inches of rain fell over a couple of days. Ramey Rd, Shady Ln, and Old Highway 441 were among the roads that were inundated by overflowing creeks.
Water at least six inches deep was observed flowing across N.C. Highway 194 South, making the road impassible until the water receded. No damage was reported to the road during this event.
The road was closed near the intersection of Route 7 and Pulaski Highway due to high water from flooding.

The Mercer County 911 Center reported that a home was flooded along the 7000 block of New Hope Road, with both lanes of the road also flooded. The water, likely from a tributary of Brush Creek rising out of its banks, was reported to be more than 6 inches deep across the road. No damage was reported to the road. The damage estimate is flood damage to the home. A little over 5 inches of rain had fallen across the local area in the 24 hours ending 11 am EDT.

A stream gauge on the Broad River at Blacksburg (gauge dropped out around 00Z on the 27th) indicated flash flooding developed along the river after extreme rainfall occurred over the headwaters across the mountains and foothills, while rainfall over Cherokee County was generally between 6 and 10 inches over two days. A portion of Little Hope Rd and River Rd was inundated, as were various secondary roads. Access roads to Cherokee Falls and Gaston Shoals dams were also inundated.

Stream gauges and emergency management indicated catastrophic flash flooding developed across portions of Burke County, mainly central and northern sections after 7-13 inches of rain fell across much of the county in three days, with some amounts over 20 inches reported in the Jonas Ridge area. Major flooding developed along multiple tributaries of the Catawba River, including Johns River, Linville River, Hunting Creek in Morganton, Lower Creek, and upper reaches of the Catawba River itself. A water level gauge at Bridgewater Dam on Lake James exceeded its record crest by more than four feet. Another gauge on Johns River north of Morganton exceeded 30 feet, which was the highest crest in the gauges history, breaking the old record of 28.6 feet (both records occurred during Hurricane Frances, 2004). Numerous homes were inundated throughout the area, particularly along the Catawba River, and dozens of homes were completely swept away. Swift water rescues were reported along the Linville River. Otherwise, numerous roads were inundated and damaged or destroyed throughout this part of the county. Several landslides were discovered in the higher terrain, primarily in remote areas of the Linville Gorge Wilderness and in the Jonas Ridge area.

The intersection of New River Parkway and Hardin Road is flooded and impassible due to nearby Brush Creek flowing out of its banks. The Creek rose quickly when a band of heavier rainfall brought 1.1 inches within a 30 minute period ending at 6:20 am EDT. No damage was reported to the road. There were unconfirmed reports of a vehicle that may have been stranded in flood waters. Rainfall rates of less than 0.10 inch per hour over the next few hours allowed the water to recede back in the banks of the creek.
Rock Creek was reported out of its banks and was flowing across Peach Bottom Road several inches deep.

The Mercer County 911 Center reports that Sparkles Road was washed out forming a deep trench and exposing a gas line. No injuries were reported, but an elderly resident need assistance to leave his home in the direct area due to the flooding. The damage estimate is the estimated cost of repairing the road.

Runoff from heavy rainfall over nearly saturated soil caused a portion of Roanoke Street to be flooded and impassible for a brief period of time. Rainfall rates at times were close to four inches per hour, with rainfall totals of around 1.5 inches falling in a 90 minute period. Crest Unit Streamflow peaked at 464 cfs/mi^2 at around 4:30 pm EDT.

A thunderstorm produced around 1.5 inches of rain falling at rates of around three inches per hour. This rain fell across ground that was very moist from rainfall occurring during Tropical Storm Helene a few days earlier. Runoff from the rainfall caused multiple roads located northwest of the town of Appomattox to become flooded and impassible with several inches of flowing water across them. This included Phelps Branch Road where it intersects Phelps Branch, as well as North Creek Road at North Creek. No damage to the roads were reported, which were open to traffic after the water receded.
Maple Creek overflowed and flooded roads in and around Mineral Springs Park.

Stream gauges and county comms reported major flash flooding developed along the headwaters of the French Broad basin after 15-22 inches of rain fell across much of the county over three days. Flash flooding first developed along the French Broad River near Rosman, where Depot St, a portion of Highway 178 near Chestnut St, and Hannah Ford Rd between Rosman and Brevard were inundated. Dozens of homes were damaged in Rosman alone, with some structures destroyed after bring inundated with several feet of water. The stream gauge on the French Broad at Rosman crested at 15.5 feet, which exceeded the record by more than a half foot (October 1964). Flooding later developed along the Davidson River toward daybreak, which damaged multiple campgrounds, low water crossings, and some structures in the Davidson River area of Pisgah National Forest, while also inundating and entering structures along portions of Davidson River Rd, Old Hendersonville Rd, Deavor Rd, and Wilson Rd in the Pisgah Forest area. Dozens of water rescues occurred in this area. Due to a combination of very heavy rainfall and backwater effects from the French Broad, the Little River inundated and damaged roads and campgrounds in Dupont State Forest and the Cedar Mountain area.

A stream gauge on the Broad River near Boiling Springs indicated flash flooding developed after extremely rainfall occurred upstream across the mountains over three days, with 4 to 8 inches fell over Cleveland Country during that time. The main impacts during this time were near Abes Mountain Rd, where numerous homes were inundated and damaged. Otherwise, numerous roads, greenway spaces, and some campgrounds were flooded. Although heavy rainfall and flash flooding ended across the area by early afternoon of the 27th, major river flooding continued along the Broad through the 28th. The river did not return to its banks until the morning of the 29th.

Collier County emergency management reported that in Marco Island an estimated 50 to 70 vehicles were stranded due to flooded roadways and there was flood water intrusion in some low-lying buildings and coastal structures up to 6 inches deep. NWS survey and damage assessments by local officials indicated that flood inundation was mainly 1-2 feet from a mix of rainfall and storm surge.

Stream gauges indicated flash flooding developed along the Tuckasegee River and some of its tributaries, including Scotts Creek in Sylva after 10 to 15 inches of rain fell across the upper part of the basin over a couple of days. 1.5 to 2.5 inches of that fell over the headwaters in less than three hours during the morning of the 27th. A portion of Highway 107 was inundated south of Cullowhee, while several homes were inundated between Cullowhee and Canada Rd. Additional structures and roads were inundated downstream in the Dillsboro and Webster areas, including Dillard Rd. Scotts Creek inundated a mobile home park and a church building off Steeple Rd in Sylva and inundated streets and briefly entered some structures in Dillsboro.
Runoff from heavy rain was observed flowing about 6 inches deep in front of the Wade Center on Highland Avenue. No damage was reported to the roadway.
Road closures were reported around the town of Janesville due to flooded roadways.

Historic, catastrophic flash flooding developed along the Broad River during the overnight and early morning hours as rainfall rates began to intensify again during the evening. The most intense rainfall occurred around sunrise, as the tropical rain bands near the center of Helene swept across the area. Dozens of structures were swept downstream and dozens more damaged during this time. Much of the Chimney Rock community was destroyed, with considerable debris swept downstream and deposited into Lake Lure. Dozens of landslides also occurred across this part of Rutherford County, especially in the upper part of the Hickory Nut Gorge. This contributed further to structural damage. Almost all of the residents of the community evacuated well before the worst of the flooding developed, but one 53-year-old woman died when her home was swept away.

Rainfall rates began to intensify as tropical rainbands near the center of Helene swept across the area during the morning hours after 10-17 inches of rain fell across much of the county, with amounts over 20 inches reported in the eastern part of the county. Devastating flash flooding developed along numerous streams, especially across the eastern half of the county. This included the French Broad River, which was already in moderate flood stage at Asheville, but began to rise rapidly during this time, culminating in historic and devastating flooding in the River Arts District, where numerous structures were inundated and damaged, and multiple structures were swept away. The Asheville gauge crested at just under 25 feet during early afternoon, exceeding the record stage by more than a foot, a record that had stood since the Great Flood of 1916. In addition, significant flooding was reported along the Ivy River in the Barnardsville community and vicinity, where multiple structures and numerous roads were inundated. The Broad River also saw significant flooding in the southeast part of the county, impacting several structures and multiple roads. Otherwise, numerous tributaries of these larger streams also overflowed their banks. More than 300 landslides were identified across Buncombe County, with some of those causing additional structural damage. Multiple fatalities were reported throughout the area, most due to drowning, but some due to landslide-related destruction. Damage to transportation infrastructure due to the combination of flooding and downed trees was widespread, with some communities inaccessible for days. Damage to the water infrastructure resulted in running water being unavailable in Asheville for days. Once the service was restored, boiling water advisories were in effect for almost two months.

Little Beaver Island Creek overflowed at least 25 feet out of its banks, and completely washed out a 30 foot wide section of Franklin Moore Road, leaving a large gap where the road used to be located. The road is completely impassible until repairs can be completed. No injuries were reported in this event. MRMS data indicated 6-hour rainfall amounts ending 9 pm EST were around 1.5 times that of 6-hour flash flood guidance, while the average recurrence interval for 6-hours was about a 25 year event.

Moore Springs Road was washed out by Cascade Creek, making the road impassible until repairs can be completed. No injuries were reported. MRMS data indicated 6-hour rainfall amounts ending 9 pm EST were 1.5 to 1.6 times that of 6-hour flash flood guidance, while the average recurrence interval for 6-hours was a 25 year event.

A stream gauge on Twelvemile Creek near Liberty indicated flash flooding developed along the stream after 11 to 17 inches of rain fell over three days, with 1 to 2 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. In addition to the creek inundating portions of Concord Church Rd and Riggins Bridge Rd, the grounds of the Pickens County Flea Market were covered with up to 5 feet of water.

Stream gauges indicated flash flooding developed over the headwaters of the Saluda River basin after 15-20 inches of rain, with locally higher amounts fell across the area over three days, with 1.5 to 3 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. The Middle Saluda and smaller tributaries overflowed their banks in the River Falls community, inundating portions of River Falls Rd, Devils Fork Rd, Oil Camp Rd, and Gap Creek Rd, where a house was inundated. Additionally, the North Saluda overflowed onto Old Settlement Rd near Highway 11 and inundated a farm off Bates Bridge Rd.

Public reported flash flooding developed across the city of Asheville and vicinity after 3 to 4 inches of rain fell in around three hours. Most of the flooding involved inundation of roads due to poor drainage. However, Reed Creek did overflow its banks in Woodfin, inundating portions of a golf course and flooding Elk Mountain Scenic Highway.

A stream gauge on Davidson River in the Pisgah Forest area indicated flash flooding developed after 4 to 5 inches of rain fell across the basin in less than 24 hours, with 1 to 2.5 inches of that falling in less than 3 hours. Davidson River Rd and Wilson Rd were inundated in Pisgah Forest. In addition, backwater effects along Turkey Creek also resulted in flooding of Deavor Rd.

Gauges across the city of Charlotte indicated flash flooding developed along multiple streams across the eastern part of the city after 4 to 7 inches fell across the county over two days, with 1-2 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. Mallard Creek flooded in the northeast part of the city, inundating a portion of Pavilion Blvd and parking lots and greenways adjacent to N Tryon St and E Mallard Creek Church Rd. Toby Creek flooded low lying areas on the UNC-Charlotte campus. Briar Creek inundated Shannonhouse Dr and flooded the parking lots of apartment buildings along Shannonhouse Dr and Dolphin Ln. Irvins Creek and tributaries inundated Sam Newell Rd and Tank Town Rd near Matthews. Graymist Drive in the far east part of the county was impassable due to water from an overflowing Caldwell Creek.

A stream gauge on the North Fork Catawba River in the North Cove community exceeded its established flood stage and indicated significant flash flooding developed after 10-17 inches fell over the watershed in about three days. Dozens of structures, roads, and campgrounds were inundated and damaged. Dozens of landslides occurred throughout the watershed, mainly in secluded areas of the Pisgah National Forest.

Stream gauges indicated flash flooding developed across western Caldwell County, particularly Johns River, Yadkin River and their tributaries after 7-12 inches fell across the western half of the county over three days. Flash flooding first developed along Wilson Creek, followed by flooding developing downstream along Johns River. After briefly subsiding during the evening, flash flooding rapidly redeveloped and became catastrophic as tropical rainbands around the remnant center of Helene swept across the area around sunrise. In addition to Wilson Creek and Johns River, major flash flooding also developed along the Yadkin River during this time. Hundreds of structures and roads were inundated and damaged or destroyed throughout the area. Several landslides were also discovered, primarily near the Avery and Watuaga County lines.

Runoff from continued heavy rain resulted in numerous roads becoming flooded and impassible across Ashe County per reports from the public and from the Ashe County 911 Dispatch Center. Rainfall totals ranging from 7 to locally 11 inches were observed across much of the county on the 26th, resulting in numerous flooded creeks, as well as several roads that were covered by several inches to feet of flowing water. After a brief lull in rainfall as the Predecessor Rainfall Event concluded early on the morning of the 27th, allowing flooding to slow down briefly, heavy rain associated with the arrival of Tropical Storm Helene moved across the county, falling at rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour. Flash flooding occurred in several communities, including in the Town of Lansing, where some buildings were flooded nearly 10 feet deep when Big Horse Creek rose out of its banks within a few hours time. Near Lansing, a landslide was observed along the 2500 block of Tucker Road, while a swift water rescue occurred just off of Highway 194 as a vehicle became stranded in flood waters. Along Cranberry Creek in the northeast corner of the county, a bridge was washed out. At least one fatality was reported when the occupant of a vehicle was swept away after becoming stranded in flood waters. Property damage and cleanup estimates are running close to 116 million dollars.
Water over the road at 12 AN RD E.
The tunnel on Old Bramwell Road under the railroad was flooded and impassible due to runoff from heavy rain. No damage was reported to the tunnel or roadway.

Reed Creek rose several feet out of its banks across Bethesda Church Road. The culvert underneath the road was completely washed out several feet downstream, causing the road to collapse and be impassible to traffic until repairs are complete. Debris lines indicate that the creek was over 80 feet wide (normally around 25 feet) at the height of the flooding event. Because of the dark, one car drove into the flood waters and became stranded, with one occupant needing rescue. No injuries were reported. MRMS data indicated 6-hour rainfall amounts ending 9 pm EDT were 1.5 to 1.6 times that of 6-hour flash flood guidance, while the average recurrence interval for 6-hours was a 25 year event.
County Road 61 washed out near I-90 just west of Alden. At least six inches of water was flowing across 850th Avenue north of Maple Island.

The Smyth County Emergency Manager reported that two residents along Flat Ridge Road were rescued from their home when water from Cressy Creek rose up into their homes. Water was 6-12 deeper than normal around the home and was still rising at the time of rescue. No injuries were reported. It is unknown if the creek water actually entered either of the homes.

A tributary of Brush Creek overflowed its banks several inches deep across Sportsman Drive near the intersection with New Hope Road, making the road impassible until the water receded. No damage was reported to the drive.
Broadcast media relayed a video of sidewalk and street flooding in the French Quarter.
Road closures were reported south of Waseca due to flooded roadways.

Stream gauges and emergency management reported catastrophic flash flooding developed along the Catawba River basin after 15-22 inches of rain fell across the western half of the county over three days. Dozens of structures were damaged or destroyed in the Old Fort area alone. Hundreds were damaged throughout the entire basin, with some structures being completely swept away. A 33-year-old woman was killed in one of these homes. Hundreds of roads were also damaged, with multiple roads completely washed out. The extreme rainfall triggered hundreds of landslides across the higher terrain in the western third of the county.

Stream gauges and the media reported catastrophic flash flooding developed along the North Pacolet and Green River basins in the western half of Polk County after 15-20 inches of rain fell across the area over three days, with 1.5 to 2.5 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th as tropical rainbands near the remnant center of Helene swept across the area. Dozens of structures were damaged or destroyed along Green River Cove Rd and along Highway 176 due to flooding along the North Pacolet. In addition to the major stream flooding, the extreme rainfall triggered dozens of landslides across the western third of the county. One of these landslides destroyed a home off Highway 176, killing a 67-year-old woman.

A thunderstorm produced around 1.5 inches of rain falling at rates exceeding four inches per hour. This rain fell across ground that was nearly saturated from rainfall during Tropical Storm Helene a few days earlier. At 6 pm EDT, FLASH CREST Unit Streamflow was as high as 400 cfs/mi^2, while the 1-hour QPE was 135 percent of FFG values. This rainfall flooded Broad Hollow Road, making it impassible until the flooding receded. No damage was reported to the road.

Historic and catastrophic flash flooding developed along multiple streams across Henderson County during the overnight and early morning hours as rainfall rates began to intensify again during the evening. Flash flooding first redeveloped along the Rocky Broad River in the Bat Cave community, but spread to encompass most of the other major streams in the county, including Mud Creek and Bat Fork in the Hendersonville area, as well as Mills River and Cane Creek. The most intense rainfall occurred around sunrise, as the tropical rain bands near the center of Helene swept across the area. Catastrophic flash flooding first developed along the Rocky Broad River and its tributary Reedypatch Creek. Numerous homes were swept away along both streams. Seven fatalities were reported in Henderson County, mostly occurring in homes that were destroyed in the Bat Cave area (F63HOU, F89HOU, M65UNK, M66HOU, F60HOU, F50HOU, M72UNK). Major flooding developed along Mud Creek and Bat Fork, with numerous businesses and other structures inundated in the Hendersonville area. Meanwhile, stream levels on the French Broad River at Fletcher, which was already in moderate flood, began to increase rapidly around sunrise, reaching major flood stage and exceeding the record stage by more than 10 feet (the gauge was installed in 2002). Numerous roads were damaged or washed out throughout the county. Three-day rainfall amounts ranged from 9-15 inches across much of the county to 15-20 inches, with locally higher amounts across the southern and eastern part of the county. Hundreds of landslides also occurred across Henderson County, especially in the eastern part of the county. This contributed further to structural damage.

River gauges and emergency management reported flash flooding developed across portions of Cabarrus County after 3 to 6 inches of rain fell across the county over two days, with 1 to 2 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. The main impacts were to the Rocky River and especially its tributaries. The Rocky River inundated several roads throughout the western and southern part of the county, including Shiloh Church Rd and Mount Pleasant Rd. In addition, Wolf Meadow Branch inundated Stough Rd, Back Creek flooded Stallings Rd, Dutch Buffalo Creek overflowed onto Bowman-Barrier Rd, and Muddy Creek inundated Hopewell Church Rd in Midland.

A stream gauge on the Catawba River indicated flash flooding developed after 5-9 inches of rain fell over the basin over two days. One to two inches of that fell in less than six hours during the morning of the 27th. The main impacts were just downstream of the Highway 21 bridge, where Herrons Ferry Rd and Brakefield Rd and adjacent parks/greenways and parking lots were inundated. Additionally, Wildcat Creek briefly overtopped its banks and inundated McConnells Highway.
Public video of water over roads.

Stream gauges indicated flash flooding developed along Durbin Creek near Fountain Inn and along Little River in Laurens after 7-10 inches of rain fell across Laurens County over three days, with 2.5 to 3.5 inches of that falling in less than 3 hours during the morning of the 27th. Durbin Creek inundated Sullivan Rd and Jones Mill Rd. Meanwhile, Little River inundated parks and greenways in Laurens.

Stream gauges reported and county comms confirmed flash flooding developed along Mud Creek after 3 to 5 inches of rain fell in the Hendersonville area in less than 12 hours, with one to 2 inches of that falling during the early morning of the 26th. Impacted roads included an access road at the intersection of S Church St and S Main St and Kanuga Rd at Erkwood Dr. Greenways and low-lying roads were also inundated farther downstream between Hendersonville and the French Broad River.

Emergency manager reported flash flooding developed along the Catawba River and some tributaries from Old Fort through the central part of the county after a swath of 3 to 4 inches of rain fell in the headwaters over 2-4 hours. Multiple campgrounds and low water crossing and secondary roads along the river were inundated. This included Parker Padgett Rd, where water rescues of motorists from several stranded vehicles occurred. Impacted tributaries included Mill Creek in the Old Fort are, which inundated part of Orchard St. In addition, Hidden Forest Drive off of Highway 221 was reportedly flooded in the Woodlawn area.

Emergency management and a stream gauge and reported flash flooding developed in the Mountain Island Lake area ater extremely heavy rainfall occurred across the headwaters of the Catawba River in the mountains and foothills over a three day period. More than a hundred homes and numerous roads downstream of the dam were inundated and damaged, especially on Lake Dr, Riverside Dr, and Riverhaven Dr. The stream level gauge at the dam crested more than a foot above the record (August 1940).

The Wilkes County 911 Dispatch Center received several reports of water flowing several inches deep across roads and bridges throughout the western half of the county as rounds of heavy rain continue to pass across the area. With seven to ten inches of rain occurring on the 26th, creeks are already swollen and soils are saturated. Even brief periods of heavy rain have resulted in rivers rapidly flowing out of their banks and roads becoming flooded and impassible. A swift water rescue was required for two occupants of a vehicle trapped in flood waters along Roaring River Road near Tyson Feed Mill. Cub Creek was also observed rising out of its banks Friday morning, covering nearly all of Cub Creek Park. Some of the roads that were observed flooded and impassible during the morning and afternoon of the 27th include: Shumate Mountain Road, Mertie Road, Cane Creek Church Road, Vannoy Road, Colvard Road, W. Country Club Drive, Casper Hawkins Road, Avery Anderson Road, Lee Mountain Road, Twin Locust Road, Arbor Grove Church Road, Moxley Road, Sandy Creek Road, Elk Creek Road, Dehart Church Road, Reservoir Road, Glenn Carlton Road, and Highway 268.

Stream gauges on the Saluda River in west Greenville and west Pelzer indicated flash flooding developed along the river after 8-15 inches of rain fell across the foothills in three days, with 1.5 to 2.5 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. Multiple homes and structures were inundated and damaged on the Anderson County side of the river from Powdersville down to Pelzer, including on Lakeview Dr, Birch River Rd, and on River Rd. A 60-year-old woman was killed when her vehicle was swept away in floodwater.

Reports from broadcast media and storm spotter of street flooding across the city of Violet with multiple cars stalled. One social media video shows water covering roadways and water approaching car doors. Time estimated from radar and from reports.

Widespread and massive flash flooding of Tuscarora Creek and surrounding tributaries devastated roads, homes and businesses between, and including, the villages of Greenwood and Jasper. Homes were pushed off foundations and were seen floating downstream smashing into area bridges. Dozens of people were rescued from flooded homes and vehicles and displaced in temporary shelters for weeks.

A tributary of Moravian Creek was out of its banks and was observed flowing several inches deep across School Street. No damage was reported to the roadway, which was open to traffic after the water receded.

Heavy rain, falling at rates of about one inch per hour, resulted in renewed flash flooding across portions of Smyth. A portion of Highway 16 was partially washed out and significantly damaged sometime during the early morning hours of the 27th, exposing multiple utility lines beneath the road surface.

Intensifying rainfall rates resulted in several creeks rising several feet out of their banks within the community of Sugar Grove. Reports were received that more than one mobile home became flooded, forcing the residents to evacuate to higher ground. Around 5 inches of rain had fallen in the 24 hours ending 12 pm on the 26th when heavier rain entered the area from the south.

Numerous reports of major flash flooding were received across Sumner County, including Gallatin. Impassable roads included Upper Station Creek Road, Liberty Lane, and Long Hollow Pike. Long Hollow Gardens and Long Hollow Golf Course were also reported to be underwater. A house along Long Hollow Gardens was also inundated with flood waters. Life-threatening flash flooding across Sumner County prompted the issuance of a Flash Flood Emergency for the county. Damages are a rough estimate.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in southern Overton County, particularly along Highway 164 between Pilgrim Circle and Memory Lane east of Monterey. Damages are unknown.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding across Putnam County, particularly in Algood where North Allen Road and Dodson Branch Highway were reported to be flooded and impassable. Damages are not known.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding across Rutherford County, particularly in the Eagleville area and south of Murfreesboro. In Eagleville, Horton Highway at Arno-Allisona Road was reported to be flooded and impassable. In Murfreesboro, Armstrong Valley Road was reported to be impassable. Unfortunately, flooding led to the indirect death of a 10-year-old child who was swept away into a storm drain while playing in the water in the streets.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Lebanon with property flooding reported along Lovers Lane in northeast Lebanon. Damages are a rough estimate.
Emergency management reported that Highway 84 between Mexia and Teague was closed due to flash flooding.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding near Sparta with Hickory Valley Road and Lost Creek Road reported to be impassable. Damages are unknown.

Numerous reports of major flooding were received across Davidson County. In Goodlettsville, the Interstate 65 onramp at Long Hollow Pike and Caldwell Drive was flooded. In Antioch, Culbertson Road was underwater while in Hermitage, Stones River Walkway was also underwater. Interstate 24 East after exit 52 was forced to close due to flooding. Damages are a rough estimate.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Bumpus Mills with flooding reported on Highway 120 and Tobacco Port Road. Damages are unknown.

Numerous reports of major flooding were received across Robertson County, including the Cross Plains area. Multiple rounds of heavy rain caused flash flooding to begin early in the morning on May 8th and continue into the overnight hours. Roads that were reported impassable included Empson Road, Covington Road, and Cross Plains Road. A water rescue had to be performed along Cross Plains Road due to the car becoming submerged in flood waters. Life-threatening flash flooding prompted the issuance of a Flash Flood Emergency for Robertson County. Damages are a rough estimate.

Heavy rain across Marshall County caused flash flooding in the area. Beasley Road in Chapel Hill was closed due to being washed out. Two water rescues had to be performed with one at a residence and the other in a vehicle. Damages are a rough estimate.

Numerous reports of major flooding were received across Robertson County, including the Springfield area. Multiple rounds of heavy rain caused flash flooding to begin early in the morning on May 8th and continue into the overnight hours. Roads that were reported impassable included New Chapal Road and Lahr Road where a water rescue had to be performed due to the car becoming submerged in flood waters. Life-threatening flash flooding prompted the issuance of a Flash Flood Emergency for Robertson County. Damages are a rough estimate.

Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Grundy County. Near Palmer, a section of Barker Cove Road was washed away. Near Beersheba Springs, Highway 56 was flooded and impassable. Damages are a rough estimate.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding at Dillon Park in Woodbury. Damages are unknown.
Emergency management reported road closures in the area south of Moody and a culvert collapse at Dowell Road.
Emergency management reported flooding in Mart. Water covered the yard of a resident and approached the house.

Numerous reports of major flooding were received across Robertson County, including the White House area. Multiple rounds of heavy rain caused flash flooding to begin early in the morning on May 8th and continue into the overnight hours. The worst flooding was reported along and south of Highway 76 with specific roadways reported impassable including Sage Road, Melton Road, and Union Road. Flooding was also reported in White House High School. Life-threatening flash flooding prompted the issuance of a Flash Flood Emergency for Robertson County. Damages are a rough estimate.
Heavy rain caused flash flooding in Stewart County with a baseball park on Highway 79 reported to be underwater. Damages are unknown.
Emergency management reported a flooded roadway and parking lot at Sterrett Road and Highway 77 in Waxahachie.
Roadway flooding near the intersection of Oklahoma Highways 18 and 105. Event time is approximate.
Roadway flooding near the intersection of U.S. Highway 81 and Oklahoma Highway 33 in the community of Kingfisher. Traffic was blocked. Event time is approximate.
Roads in the area were entirely covered with at least 6 inches of water.

Numerous reports of flash flooding were received across Montgomery County, especially in the Clarksville area. Several roadways across the county were reported to be flooded and impassable, including Trenton Road. Damages are a rough estimate.

Numerous reports of major flooding were received across Robertson County, including the Greenbrier area. Multiple rounds of heavy rain caused flash flooding to begin early in the morning on May 8th and continue into the overnight hours. One home on Old Greenbrier Pike at Worsham Springs was reported to be surrounded by water. Life-threatening flash flooding prompted the issuance of a Flash Flood Emergency for Robertson County. Damages are a rough estimate.
Emergency management reported several roads closed and county roads with culverts washed out.
Roadway flooding along portions of Lakeview Road. Event time is approximate.

Emergency management reported multiple instances of flash flooding along Highway 317 from Temple to the McLennan County line; including impassable roads and at least one vehicle stranded in high water.
Fire and rescue reported that Bushy Creek had overflowed its banks, flooding 3 or 4 homes along FM 1240. This required the evacuation of residents in the flooded homes.

Historically bad flash flooding across Roswell, reported by numerous emergency officials and the public. Thunderstorms training over Roswell dumped an all-time one-day rainfall record of 5.78 at the Roswell Airport with numerous other public weather stations across town ranging from 4 to 9 inches. Major flooding was reported across the city and nearby low-lying areas south and west of town. Numerous vehicles were submerged in over 4 feet of water while several more were swept away. The Roswell Daily Record reported that as many as 500 rescues were carried out over the weekend during and after the flooding. Estimates have as many as 400 homes and 200 businesses facing significant damage. The Roswell Convention Center was hosting a UFO festival when flood waters up to 5 feet entered the building. Attendees were being rescued from the rooftop. Roswell's Spring River Zoo also suffered extensive damage including the loss of one donkey. Flood damage was also sustained to Roswell's Landfill and Wastewater Treatment Plant. All roads entering the city were closed by State Police. The city lost 4 fire trucks and 7 police patrol cars with numerous city facilities damaged. There is one confirmed direct fatality from drowning and one indirect fatality from a heart attack reported and there may have been more as many vehicles were swept away along the Spring River drainage.
